title: The case for an older Giza
about: The guided tour. Each stop names a station, the eras it runs through in order (the first shown on arrival, the rest glided or cut to in turn, each held once it is on screen), where the view turns (degrees: yaw from north, pitch above the horizon, vertical field of view), an optional overlay from overlays.json (written by render/publish.py from the database and the claims engine) and an optional figure featured after the eras. `text` is the card's lead, kept short; `detail` and `who` sit under Read more. Figures in `numbers` are the project's own, from docs/dossier.md, docs/shafts.md and the sky page; the arguments are the proponents', put at their strongest.

stops.summary: The plateau runs back from today to 10,500 BCE, and the case is set out.
stops.title: The case for an older Giza
text: The record dates Giza to Egypt's Fourth Dynasty, around 2560 BCE. Graham Hancock, Robert Bauval, the geologist Robert Schoch and John Anthony West argue that the plateau is far older: that its plan, its alignments and some of its stones go back to around 10,500 BCE, the age they identify with Zep Tepi, the Egyptians' own "First Time".
Watch the plateau run back to it.
detail: This tour puts their case at its strongest, one station at a time, with the project's own measurements beside each argument. The eras you will see: today, as surveyed; Khufu's Giza as built, a reconstruction; and two theorized ages, the long rains of about 7000 BCE and the First Time.
stops.who: West, Serpent in the Sky (1979) · Hancock, Fingerprints of the Gods (1995) · Hancock and Bauval, Keeper of Genesis (1996)

stops.summary: Schoch's geology: the Sphinx worn by rain, not wind.
stops.title: Weathered by rain
text: If rain did this, the Sphinx was old before Khafre. In 1991 the geologist Robert Schoch argued that the deep, rounded hollows worn into the Sphinx's body, layer by layer, and the fissures in the walls of its ditch were cut by rain running down the rock for thousands of years, not by wind-blown sand. Egypt's last long wet age ended well before 2500 BCE.
Watch the fresh-cut lion wear under the long rains, then see the body as it stands today, its flank cut back in deep layers.
stops.numbers: Schoch's estimate for the carving of the core body: 7000 to 5000 BCE at the latest. West and Hancock argue for the eleventh millennium BCE.
detail: Seismic soundings Schoch made with Thomas Dobecki found the weathering under the floor of the ditch deeper in front of the Sphinx than behind it. He read this as the front being cut first, long before the rest.
stops.who: Schoch, Redating the Great Sphinx of Giza, KMT (1992) · Dobecki and Schoch, Geoarchaeology (1992) · West (1979)

stops.summary: Hundred-tonne blocks from the Sphinx's ditch, faced later in granite.
stops.title: Megaliths from the Sphinx's own quarry
text: Beside the Sphinx stand two temples, Khafre's valley temple and the Sphinx Temple. Their cores are built of limestone blocks cut from the Sphinx's own ditch, some estimated at over a hundred tonnes; Hancock puts the largest at two hundred.

Schoch and West argue that this limestone carries the same rain weathering as the ditch, and that the red granite you see here was cut on its back to fit surfaces that had already worn. The temples, they say, were old when Khafre faced them.

figure.alt: Huge limestone core blocks of the Sphinx Temple, their faces cut back in uneven horizontal layers, stacked in a wall beside the Sphinx's ditch.
figure.caption: Next door, the Sphinx Temple's core today, from the ditch at the Sphinx's paws: blocks of the ditch's own limestone, their beds worn back in layers. A reconstruction; the blocks' sizes and wear are look choices after photographs.

stops.summary: A head too small, and a lion facing the dawn of the Age of Leo.
stops.title: The lion faces the lion
text: The Sphinx's head is small for its body, and West and others read it as a recut. Hancock and Bauval argue the statue began as a lion, gazing due east to where the sun rises at the equinoxes, and that around 10,500 BCE the constellation rising behind that sun was Leo: a lion facing the dawn of the Age of the Lion.
Watch the king's head give way to that lion.
stops.numbers: Spring equinox, 10,500 BCE: the sun rose at 89°31′, with Regulus, Leo's brightest star, 50 minutes ahead of it. The lion is a stand-in fitted to the Sphinx's outline.
detail: Because the Earth's axis slowly wobbles, the constellation behind the equinox sunrise changes, one sign in about 2,150 years. Today it is Pisces; in Khafre's day it was Taurus, the bull. The last time a lion stood on that horizon was around 10,500 BCE.

figure.alt: The spring equinox dawn of 10,500 BCE seen from behind the lion: Leo stretched along the eastern horizon above the point where the sun is about to rise.
figure.caption: From behind the lion at the spring equinox of 10,500 BCE: Leo lies along the dawn horizon, the sun about to rise beneath it.

more.label: Leo on the dawn horizon, on the sky page

stops.who: West (1979) · Hancock and Bauval, Keeper of Genesis (1996)

stops.summary: The midsummer sun sets between two pyramids: the horizon hieroglyph.
stops.title: The sun in the horizon sign
text: Seen from the Sphinx at midsummer, the sun goes down in the gap between the Great Pyramid and Khafre's. The two pyramids become the two hills of akhet, the hieroglyph for the horizon, with the sun's disc between them, and the Sphinx lies before them on guard.
The line drawn here runs from the Sphinx to that sunset, in 2500 BCE: monuments credited to different kings, composed as one image of the sky.
stops.numbers: The midsummer sun set at 298.5° from the Sphinx; the middle of the gap is at 295.9°, about five sun-widths away.
detail: The Egyptologist Mark Lehner reads the plateau as this single sign. For the case for an older Giza it is a mark of one plan behind monuments credited to different kings: a design, they argue, that came first.
stops.who: Lehner, The Complete Pyramids (1997) · Lehner and Hawass, Giza and the Pyramids (2017)

stops.summary: Bauval's correlation, with the belt at its lowest in 10,450 BCE.
stops.title: Orion's belt on the ground
text: In 1994 Robert Bauval proposed that the three pyramids are laid out as Orion's belt: two stars nearly in line and a fainter third set off to one side, as Menkaure's smaller pyramid is. As the sky precesses the belt climbs and sinks; it stood at its lowest around 10,450 BCE, and that, Bauval and Hancock argue, is the moment the plan records.
Watch the sky drop from 2450 to 10,450 BCE.
stops.numbers: Fitted on the ground, the three stars land 7.5, 14.9 and 7.4 m from the pyramids' centres across 936 m, once the belt is turned 13° to match.
detail: To the Egyptians Orion was Osiris, god of death and rebirth. In 10,450 BCE Alnitak crossed the meridian 9°13′ above the horizon, the lowest of its 26,000-year swing.

figure.alt: The three pyramids from straight above with Orion's belt laid over them and fitted, with an inset chart of the belt's angle through precession.
figure.caption: Orion's belt laid on the plan of the three pyramids: Alnitak on Khufu, Alnilam on Khafre, Mintaka on Menkaure.

more.label: The belt fitted to the plan, on the sky page

stops.who: Bauval and Gilbert, The Orion Mystery (1994) · Hancock and Bauval (1996)

stops.summary: Four shafts, four stars, and a monument to an older moment.
stops.title: Shafts aimed at the stars
text: Narrow shafts climb from the King's and Queen's Chambers through the masonry; the line follows this one up from the south wall. Measured by Rudolf Gantenbrink's robot in 1993, all four point at stars crossing the meridian around 2450 BCE: Orion's belt and Sirius to the south, Thuban and Kochab to the north.
Why does 2450 BCE help the older case? Because, Bauval argues, the same builders laid the pyramids out as Orion's belt stood in 10,450 BCE: a monument of one age built to record another.
stops.numbers: Around 2450 BCE each star crosses within 0°40′ of its shaft: Alnitak 0°12′, Sirius 0°15′, Kochab 0°14′, Thuban 0°39′.
detail: In 1964 the astronomer Virginia Trimble and the architect Alexander Badawy were the first to show that the King's Chamber's southern shaft pointed at Orion's belt as it crossed the meridian.

figure.alt: The Great Pyramid from the east, its casing seen through, its four shafts carried out into the sky to Orion's belt, Sirius, Thuban and Kochab.
figure.caption: The four shafts carried out into the sky of 2450 BCE: Alnitak and Sirius to the south, Thuban and Kochab to the north.

more.label: The shafts and their stars, on the sky page

stops.who: Badawy and Trimble (1964) · Gantenbrink (1993) · Bauval and Gilbert (1994)

stops.summary: An unfinished chamber in the bedrock, and a passage aimed at the pole star.
stops.title: The chamber under the rock
text: Thirty metres under the pyramid lies a chamber cut into the bedrock and never finished: a rough floor, a pit, a blind passage. Some who argue for an older Giza ask whether it belonged to a sacred site the pyramid was later built over.

The passage that leads down here points at the sky. The line drawn here runs up it towards the north, where Thuban, the pole star of its age, stood at its lowest: first near 3409 BCE, long before the pyramid's conventional date.
stops.numbers: The passage slopes at 26°31′. Thuban's lowest crossing of the meridian reaches that height twice: near 3409 BCE, some eight centuries before Khufu, and again near 2185 BCE.
detail: When Colonel Vyse surveyed the pyramid in the 1830s, the astronomer John Herschel pointed out that the pole star of the age would have shone straight down the passage at its lowest crossing of the meridian.

more.label: The claim computed, with both dates

stops.who: Herschel, in Vyse, Operations Carried On at the Pyramids of Gizeh (1840) · Smyth (1864)

stops.summary: True north, pi, phi and the 1:43,200 scale of the Earth.
stops.title: The shape of the Earth
text: The Great Pyramid's sides run within four arcminutes of true north. Its proportions, drawn on the face here, carry pi and the golden ratio, and Hancock finds a scale: its height times 43,200 is the Earth's polar radius, its perimeter times 43,200 the equator.

Why 43,200? It is 600 times 72, and 72 years is about how long the sky takes to precess one degree. Builders who knew the Earth's size and the sky's slow clock were not, he argues, a young civilisation.
stops.numbers: True north: 3′54″ off. Perimeter over height: 6.2850 against 2π, 6.2832. Slant height over half the side: 1.6187 against φ, 1.6180.
detail: On this reading the pyramid is a model of the northern hemisphere, drawn to the scale of the sky's own clock.
stops.who: Hancock (1995) · Tompkins, Secrets of the Great Pyramid, with Stecchini (1971)

stops.summary: The Younger Dryas, Göbekli Tepe and a lost chapter of history.
stops.title: A lost chapter
text: Hancock's larger argument is that these clues point to a civilisation lost at the end of the last Ice Age, when the Younger Dryas, 12,900 to 11,700 years ago, swung the climate and the melting ice raised the seas by over a hundred metres.
Göbekli Tepe in Turkey, great carved pillars raised around 9500 BCE, shows that monumental building at that age is no longer unthinkable. Now walk the plateau yourself.
detail: Its survivors, he proposes, carried their knowledge of the sky to those who came after, and the plateau's plan is their record. Every station can be seen in every era it was rendered in.

figure.alt: The three Giza pyramids, cased white with gold caps, rising from a tropical forest beside a flooded valley, seen from the air.
figure.caption: The First Time from the air, as the case for an older Giza imagines it: the three pyramids cased and gold-capped above a green valley.

stops.who: Hancock, Magicians of the Gods (2015) · Schmidt, Göbekli Tepe excavations (from 1995)
